Field surveys of juvenile recruitment across the central Pacific indicate that the total length at which these fish first attain sexual maturity is 26 centimeters [Lp = 26 centimeters]. The body mass corresponding to this pubertal length, derived from established length-weight relationships for the species, is approximately 244 grams [Wwp = approximately 244 grams], representing a substantial increase from the larval stage. Growing juveniles exhibit characteristic color pattern shifts that coincide with this transition, rendering them more conspicuous to conspecifics as they approach adulthood. The onset of gonadal activity at this length is consistent across much of the species range, though local resource availability may influence the exact timing of this developmental milestone.

Fully grown adults of Chlorurus spilurus can reach an ultimate total length of 48.6 centimeters [Li = 48.6 centimeters], a size that places them among the medium-bodied members of the genus. The maximum wet weight associated with this asymptotic length is approximately 1,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,600 grams], a value derived from morphometric data collected from specimens across the species' geographic distribution. The transition from sub-adult to adult body plan involves continued somatic investment, with the ultimate body mass being roughly six and a half times the weight recorded at puberty. This pronounced post-pubertal growth is typical of iteroparous reef fishes that continue to increase in size throughout much of their reproductive lifespan. Large adults are readily identifiable by their distinctive drab greenish-brown coloration, a marked departure from the mottled patterns seen in younger conspecifics, and they often occupy overlapping home ranges in areas of high coral cover.

Observational data from the northern Great Barrier Reef suggest that females participate in roughly three spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly three spawning events per year], with each event involving the release of a substantial clutch. This moderate reproductive frequency is balanced by the relatively large body size of adults, which allows for the production of numerous oocytes during each spawning aggregation. The species aggregates predictably around reef channel entrances during outgoing spring tides, a behavior that facilitates gamete mixing and reduces predation risk on spawning individuals.

Individuals in protected marine reserves may exceed this typical lifespan, with anecdotal reports of specimens reaching eight or nine years of age in areas closed to fishing. The species' reliance on complex reef structure for shelter and foraging means that habitat degradation poses a greater threat to population persistence than elevated natural mortality rates. Age determination through otolith micro-increment analysis has validated the annual periodicity of growth bands in this species, providing a reliable method for estimating population age structure.
